newsitem.title: USA: US OMB does not dispute report on Clinton tax plan.
newsitem.headline: US OMB does not dispute report on Clinton tax plan.

text.p: The Office of Management and Budget said Thursday it did not dispute the Joint Committee on Taxation's finding that President Clinton's budget would yield a $13 billion tax increase in five years, but the reasons behind it were technical.

Legislative language was sent to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) that would terminate key tax cuts at the end of 2000 and cut spending 2.25 percent in fiscal years 2001 and 2002 so that the CBO would determine that the president's budget balanced in 2002, OMB spokesman Larry Haas said.
CBO's economic assumptions were more conservative than OMB's and the White House had made a commitment that Clinton's budget would balance using either assumptions, Haas said.

For the budget to balance under CBO's projections, the legislative language had to terminate the tax cuts and cut spending, he said, adding that he did not expect that to be what would ultimately be enacted.
"They (Congress) can use any set of economic and technical assumptions they want; they can use CBO's if they choose. We think they should use OMB's," Haas said.
"So we don't think they will need to do this, but we're going the extra mile and making sure that CBO will score our budget as being balanced," he said.
Using OMB's estimates, Clinton's budget would result in a $5 billion net tax cut in fiscal 2002, Haas said.
"This is largely a technical matter," he said. "As a real world matter we do not believe the tax cuts would end," Haas said.
